# R6 Digest — Part 2e (Jer 21–24) + Ch 25 hinge

**Source:** Goldingay, NICOT *The Book of Jeremiah* — Part 2e “On Kings and Prophets” (21:1–24:10) and “An Interim Conclusion” (25:1–38).  
**Slice:** `R6_p2e_25_13262-16696.txt` (raw lines 13262–16696).  
**Coverage note:** Body commentary for 21–24 ≈ slice ll. 1–1447; ch 25 hinge ≈ ll. 2929–3337. Intermediate lines (≈1450–2927) are largely endnote/apparatus ballast (earlier-chapter footnotes), not sequential body prose on 21–25.  
**Not present in range:** Explicit comparison with Lalleman’s 23–29 structural block (Goldingay states ch 25 as hinge/axis without naming Lalleman). Lalleman-de Winkel appears only in a footnote citation (slice ~l. 2123) on prophetic tradition, not as structural foil.  
**Priority themes extracted:** kings oracles; branch/righteous shoot; good/bad figs (24); ch 25 hinge (604; MT/LXX; seventy years; nations cup).

## Claims

### C-R6-01
- **Claim:** Goldingay frames Jer 21–24 as Part 2e, a compilation with double focus on Judah’s kings and prophets—“foremost a treatise on leadership.” If 18–20 was climax, 21–24 can look like appendix/sidebar before 25, but it continues the scroll’s questions about objects of trust: kings and prophets might be hoped-for objects of trust but are “the guilty men,” cause of imminent fall. City/people messages interweave so neither leaders alone nor people alone escape judgment; addressees of part 2e are the entire people.
- **Quote:** "Jeremiah 21–24 is foremost a treatise on leadership." … "kings and prophets are the guilty men."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1–4; Part 2e intro
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-02
- **Claim:** Structurally, 21–24 begins and ends with Zedekiah-era material (sword/hunger/epidemic; dire vs good fate). Two major parts: 21:1–23:8 about kings (and people)—Zedekiah first, non-chronological; 23:9–24:10 about prophets (and people)—no names, though 27–29 associates prophetic tension with Zedekiah. After 587 the unit explains the dire fate; promises for kings (23:5–6) and people (23:7–8; 24:4–7) gain special significance.
- **Quote:** "Jeremiah 21–24 as a whole begins and ends with sections relating to the time of Zedekiah, Judah’s last king, with the threat of sword, hunger, and epidemic, and with a contrast between Yahweh planning a dire fate rather than a good one and a good one rather than a dire one."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 6–18; Part 2e outline
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-03
- **Claim:** Goldingay stresses vocation and failure of the Davidic line: five references to David’s throne/household/tree (21:12; 22:2, 4, 30; 23:5) vs only two in Jer 2–20. The tradition “singles out the Davidic kings … as the primary architects of the national calamity of 587”; they turned gift into guarantee. Treatment that begins with Zedekiah almost ends with him (23:5–6)—movie technique: show destination then backtrack.
- **Quote:** "Jeremiah 21–24 is concerned with the vocation and failure of the Davidic line, with its having turned the gift into a guarantee." … "The Jeremiah tradition singles out the Davidic kings … as the primary architects of the national calamity of 587."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 25–31; kings intro
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-04
- **Claim:** On 21:1–10 (Zedekiah under siege): first time the scroll is amid actual events (not “as if”), maybe late 589/early 588. Zedekiah sends Pashhur ben Malkiah and Zephaniah the priest to *inquire* (*dāraš*—oracle + intercession) whether Yahweh will act with extraordinary deeds (*niplāʾōt*) as in exodus/Hezekiah–Sennacherib. Irony with prior Pashhur who silenced Jeremiah. Goldingay notes no negative comment on Zedekiah in this section.
- **Quote:** "Here for the first time we are in the midst of actual events." … "Inquire (dāraš) suggests 'both oracle and intercession'… Zedekiah is asking Jeremiah to pray for the city."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 194–196; on 21:1–2
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-05
- **Claim:** Yahweh’s reply reverses exodus holy-war motifs: he turns Judah’s weapons/gathers Chaldeans into the city; *I myself will do battle with you* with outstretched hand/strong arm, anger/fury/rage (Deut 29:27 warning); epidemic then sword/hunger; no spare/pity/compassion via Nebuchadrezzar. God as main foe of his people. Message not post-fall vaticinium; actual 587 capture of Zedekiah was if anything worse.
- **Quote:** "The prophet introduces a completely opposite notion in which God is the main foe of His people." … "'If God be against us …' Nebuchadnezzar is the least of their problems."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 198–206; on 21:3–7
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-06
- **Claim:** 21:8–10 reworks Deut 30:15, 19 as *path to life / path to death* (Jeremiah alone uses that pair explicitly): life = go out and fall away to the blockading Chaldeans (“Choose exile and live!”); death = stay in city (sword/hunger/epidemic). Stance is theological not pro-Babylonian politics; elsewhere Babylon is judged at length. Fire threat recurs 21:12, 14; 22:7.
- **Quote:** "'Choose exile and live!' seems to be Jeremiah’s call to the people" … "Jeremiah is not pro-Babylonian as a political stance; his stance is a theological position."

### C-R6-07
- **Claim:** David’s household oracles (21:11–22:9): primary royal duty is *mišpāṭ*—make decisions in the morning with authority; snatch the robbed from the fraud. 2 Sam 7 promise not unconditional; Pss 72; 132 imply implementing faithful authority. Greatest concentration of *mišpāṭ* in these king sections. 22:1–5 adds resident alien/fatherless/widow, no innocent blood; conditional promise of Davidic procession through palace gateways vs ruin-oath.
- **Quote:** "Among all the commandments that might have been cited in these oracles against the kings, repeatedly choosing those that have to do with the exercise of abusive power against the weak and needy is remarkable."

- **Claim:** Coniah/Jehoiachin (22:24–30): even if he were Yahweh’s signet on the right hand, Yahweh would tear him off; mother also hurled to foreign land; register as *ʿărîrî* (deprived/childless-for-throne)—no offspring will sit on David’s throne. ### C-R6-12
- **Claim:** 23:1–8 closes kings collection with three promises that underplay future kingship: (1) shepherds plural / Yahweh as chief shepherd gathering remainder; (2) faithful shoot for David; (3) new exodus formula. Matches prior denial that Jehoiachin’s line sits the throne: David promise must stand, but *when/how* not preoccupation—focus is good shepherding and gathering exiles. Partial Second Temple fulfillments (return; leaders Sheshbazzar–Nehemiah; Zerubbabel near “shoot” in Zech 6) without equating to full messianic claim—“messianic” unwise term for Jeremiah’s promises.
- **Quote:** "Thus the promise section as a whole underplays any promise of a future king in a way that matches what precedes: no descendant of Jehoiachin will occupy David’s throne. Yahweh’s promise to David must stand, but when and how it may find fulfillment is not to be a preoccupation."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 905–907; on 23:1–8 intro
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-13
- **Claim:** Shepherds (23:1–4): Judah’s own shepherds wipe out/scatter Yahweh’s flock (like foreign shepherds); *pāqad* paronomasia—they did not attend, so Yahweh attends to them; then he himself collects remainder (*šәʾērît* now positive), returns to habitat, fruitfulness (Gen 1 / Exod 1), sets up proper shepherds so sheep fear no more.
- **Quote:** "The horrible irony here is that Judah’s own shepherds have been behaving like the foreign shepherd/kings (6:3; 12:10). Leaders easily become misleaders."

### C-R6-14
- **Claim:** **Faithful/righteous shoot** (23:5–6): first strongly positive Davidide promise in the scroll (recurs 33:14–16). *Days are coming* = definite but undated; “decisive break” in Davidic history, no bridge of historical probability from present. Shoot (*ṣemaḥ*) is *ṣaddîq*—faithful; will reign with understanding and exercise faithful authority. Name *yhwh ṣidqēnû* (“Yahweh is our faithfulness”) smirks at Zedekiah (*ṣidqîyāhû*, “Yahweh is my faithfulness”); LXX Iōsedek tightens the reversal. Plural “our” involves the audience. Not only one king but possibly a new royal line. Judah finds deliverance; Israel/Ephraim dwells in confidence.
- **Quote:** "I will set up for David a faithful shoot." … "this king’s name will be Yahweh is our faithfulness (yhwh ṣidqēnû); attentive hearers who know Zedekiah smirk again. LXX encourages the smirk by making the name Iōsedek, a more precise reversal of its Sedekia."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 952–955; on 23:5–6
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-15
- **Claim:** New-exodus oath formula (23:7–8): people will no longer swear by Yahweh who brought Israel from Egypt but by Yahweh who brought offspring from the northern country and all exile lands; they will live on their soil. Variant of 16:14–15; in LXX these verses follow v. 40. Second Temple saw partial not spectacular fulfillment—exodus still celebrated.
- **Quote:** "People did not stop celebrating the exodus in favor of celebrating the return from exile, and that return was not as spectacular as the departure from Egypt… But Yahweh did make it possible for people to come back, and they did live on their soil."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 957; on 23:7–8
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-16
- **Claim:** Prophets block (23:9–40): after kings interweaving, prophets section concentrates on prophets then Judah (24). Discerning true/false prophecy is characteristic Israelite problem, acute 597–587; likely compiled under Zedekiah not post-587 (when disagreeing disaster-prophets ceased). Theology of the word emerges once “word of Yahweh” is present. Jeremiah must distance from other prophets who look/sound like him (cf. Hananiah, ch 28).
- **Quote:** "In Israel, the problem of discerning between prophets who do and who do not speak truly was an issue more or less ever since prophecy came into being and up until the destruction of Jerusalem… Jeremiah 27–29 portrays it as particularly a problem between 597 and 587."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1219–1225; on 23:9–40 intro
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-17
- **Claim:** True vs false prophecy criteria are theological/moral, not subjective experience: *šālôm*-prophets fill with emptiness, vision from their mind not Yahweh’s mouth, promise well-being to those who disown Yahweh. True prophet has stood in Yahweh’s *sôd* (cabinet/assembly). Logic inverted: confrontational wrath-message proves cabinet attendance, not vice versa. They run unsent; fail to get people to turn—so Yahweh’s anger does not turn. Dreams: Jeremiah unfailingly negative (contrast Joel); dream vs message = straw vs grain; message like fire/hammer. Steal words; utter false “affirmation”; *maśśāʾ* (burden) wordplay—people are the burden Yahweh will hurl away.
- **Quote:** "The First Testament assumes that telling true from false prophecy is not so difficult, because the criteria for the discernment are theological and moral." … "The logic is, 'I have delivered a message about Yahweh’s wrath against the adulterous community, which is how you can know that I have been in attendance at Yahweh’s cabinet.'"
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1288–1326; on 23:16–40
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-19
- **Claim:** **Two lots of figs (24:1–10):** prose vision after 597 exile of Jeconiah and leadership. Good figs = Judahite exile group in Chaldea—Yahweh regards them *for good*, sets eye for good, return, build/not smash, plant/not pull up (echo 1:10). Will give mind to acknowledge Yahweh; covenant formula people/God; they turn with entire mind. Dire figs = Zedekiah, officials, remainder in land, and Egypt-dwellers—horror/reviling/sword-hunger-epidemic until end from the land. “Good/dire” = destiny more than inherent moral quality; no desert differential. Confronts Jerusalem assumption that stay-behinds are vindicated and 597 exiles condemned; parallels Ezek 11. Links prospectively to 27–29 (29:17–19 variant).
- **Quote:** "exile does not seal its victims’ fate." … "There is no basis for distinguishing between what each community deserves. The point of the message is to get home to the Jerusalemites the inevitability of their paying the price for their wrongdoing if they continue in it, though also to hint at the basis for hope."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1362–1448; on 24:1–10
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[new-covenant]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-21
- **Claim:** **Ch 25 as hinge/axis (priority):** Goldingay titles it “An Interim Conclusion (25:1–38 [LXX 25:1–13; 32:1–24]).” Dates to **604** (fourth year of Jehoiakim = first year of Nebuchadrezzar), ~twenty-three years after commission—midpoint of activity (mid-620s–mid-580s). Though seventeen years remain until 587, 604 is year of burning first scroll (Jer 36) and **point of no return**. Marks: (a) halfway point of the scroll; (b) transition poetry-dominated → story-dominated chapters; (c) “hinge” / “central axis around which the entire book revolves”; (d) shift from disaster-dominated half toward more restoration promises (with caveats: 26–29 then 30–33; 34–44 then 45–51; 52 mixed).
- **Quote:** "The chapter is a 'hinge' in the scroll, 'the central axis around which the entire book revolves.'" … "604 saw the burning of Jeremiah’s first, cumulative scroll (Jer 36) and thus saw Judah’s reaching what will turn out to be the point of no return."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 2929–2932; ch 25 intro
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]], [[lalleman-jeremiah-lamentations-totc]]

### C-R6-22
- **Claim:** **MT/LXX divergence at ch 25 is the most spectacular in Jeremiah:** after MT 25:1–14, LXX places six chapters of oracles against nations (= MT 46–51); detailed MT/LXX differences especially dense in ch 25 (usually LXX shorter). Possibilities: MT expansion of LXX *Vorlage*, LXX abbreviation of MT, or independent recensions. MT’s three sections look like originally separate messages joined by curators—all declare calamity for Jerusalem and other peoples by different means: 1–14 prose climactic warning; 15–29 chalice; 30–38 poetry on nations.
- **Quote:** "Jeremiah 25 marks the most spectacular divergence between MT and LXX of Jeremiah. After vv. 1–14 in MT, there appear in LXX six chapters declaring how Yahweh will bring calamity on other nations—chapters that appear as Jer 46–51 in MT."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 2934; ch 25 intro / MT–LXX
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-23
- **Claim:** 25:1–14 climactic review: twenty-three years of assiduous speaking; people have not listened; recycling phrases from 7, 16, 18 etc. Nebuchadrezzar first named as the northern enemy (cf. unnamed 1:14; 13:20); called **my servant**—shocking transfer of servant title from Davidides who became rebels; instrumental not intimate; reproach to Judah for ignoring real servants; limited duration of service. Yahweh will *devote* (*ḥāram*) country/people—holy-war motif reversed onto Judah. Sound of millstones and light of lamp (with groom/bride) = end of entire community life.
- **Quote:** "A revolutionary new statement comes in the description of Nebuchadrezzar King of Babylon … as my servant" … "theologically, Jeremiah is both pro- and anti-Babylonian; Babylon is 'both Yahweh’s servant (v. 9), and the one destined to drink last of all from the cup of wrath (v. 26).'"
- **Locus:** slice ll. 3079–3088; on 25:1–11
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-24
- **Claim:** **Seventy years (25:11b–12):** limit on Babylon’s suzerainty over the nations (not primarily a term for Judahite exile length as such, though reception so uses it). Seventy = full/substantial not infinite number; not precision (69 vs 71). Parallel to Marduk’s seventy-year waste of Babylon in Assyrian inscription (later changed)—Jeremiah’s point includes that Yahweh is not randomly fickle. Actual ~seventy-year Babylonian hegemony encouraged later reflection; becomes term for Israel’s affliction in 2 Chron 36:21; Zech 1:12; 7:5; Dan 9:2. At fulfillment Yahweh attends to Babylon/Chaldea for waywardness; desolation; “this document” = whole Jeremiah scroll (or, where LXX places OAN, those chapters).
- **Quote:** "Yahweh’s promise relates directly not to the Judahites’ time in Babylon but to the time of Babylon’s ruling the world." … "Seventy suggests a full number… a substantial number but not an infinite one. Babylon will rule the nations for so long that hardly anyone alive will see the end of that rule, but its end will come."
- **Locus:** slice ll. 3089–3092; on 25:11b–14
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-25
- **Claim:** **Nations cup / chalice (25:15–29 [LXX 32:1–15]):** visionary-symbolic action (appeal to imagination, not public acted sign): chalice of wine (fury) makes nations drink, reel, go crazy under the sword. Judah first in the list—listeners hoping for others’ doom get “same old.” Then Egypt, Philistines, Edom/Moab/Ammon, Tyre/Sidon, desert peoples, Elam/Media, northern kings—all kingdoms of earth; **Sheshach** (atbash for Babylon) drinks last (LXX lacks Sheshach line). *Qal wahomer*: if Yahweh begins with city over which his name is proclaimed, nations cannot claim freedom from guilt. Universal judgment in history, not “apocalyptic.” Treaty-curse / common-cup background possible.
- **Quote:** "Get this chalice of wine (fury) from my hand and make them drink it, all the nations that I am sending you to." … "And the king of Sheshach, he will drink after them." … "if Yahweh is bringing dire trouble on his own city, how can he stop there when other peoples are just as deserving?"
- **Locus:** slice ll. 3097–3186; on 25:15–29
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R6-26
- **Claim:** 25:30–38 poetry: third declaration of calamity with stress mainly on nations (Judah understated). Yahweh as lion roaring from on high / sacred lair against his habitat; shout like grape-treaders to all earth; argument against nations; all flesh under authority; faithless given to sword. Big storm from furthest parts; unburied dead as manure; shepherds/lords of flock howl, slaughtered/scattered, no escape; pastures of *šālôm* destroyed; lion leaves lair—desolation. Closes first half of scroll with “solemn and horrifying emphasis on Yahweh’s destructive wrath”—universal judgment day in present history (cf. Matt 24–25; 2 Thess 1).

### C-R6-27
- **Claim:** **Structural tension note (for integration with Lalleman):** Goldingay’s own architecture places Jer 21–24 as discrete Part 2e (kings + prophets) and **ch 25 as interim conclusion / hinge / central axis** closing the first half before story-heavy material. He does **not** in this range group 23–29 as one structural block or name Lalleman’s TOTC outline. Any Lalleman 23–29 framing that folds prophets through post-25 narrative with ch 25 as mid-unit rather than book-hinge would stand in tension with Goldingay’s explicit hinge/axis claim—record as commentator disagreement, not adjudicated here. (Lalleman-de Winkel cited only for prophetic-tradition comparison in out-of-body footnote ballast.)
- **Quote:** "If Jer 18–20 was a climax to the scroll so far, then Jer 21–24 might be seen as an appendix or sidebar before we come to Jer 25." … [ch 25:] "The chapter is a 'hinge' in the scroll, 'the central axis around which the entire book revolves.'"
- **Locus:** slice ll. 4, 2929–2932; structure
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]], [[lalleman-jeremiah-lamentations-totc]]
